title: Marriage, Children, and the Rich Young Man
summary: Leaving Galilee for the last time, Jesus is tested by Pharisees on divorce and answers from God's design at creation, adding that some renounce marriage for the kingdom. He welcomes little children, and he tells a rich young man to sell his possessions and follow him, which the man cannot do. Jesus warns how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom, says that with God all things are possible, and promises that those who have left everything for him will receive far more.
story: Chapter 19 opens a new stage. The phrase “When Jesus had finished saying these things” closes the community discourse of chapter 18, and Jesus leaves Galilee and heads toward Jerusalem, where he will die. From here to chapter 20 the disciples are being taught on the road. The topics are the stuff of ordinary life (marriage, children, money), and in each case Jesus overturns the accepted order. Marriage is not a contract easily dissolved but a union God has made. Children, who had no status, are the model for receiving the kingdom. Wealth, which many saw as a sign of God's blessing, can be an obstacle to it. The chapter ends with a saying, the first will be last and the last first, that the parable of chapter 20 will illustrate.
historical:
Judea beyond the Jordan refers to Perea, the region east of the river, which with Galilee was ruled by Herod Antipas. Pilgrims from Galilee to Jerusalem often traveled this way, avoiding Samaria. The Pharisees' question in verse 3 reflects a real debate of the period about Deuteronomy 24:1, which assumes that a man may divorce his wife if he finds some indecency in her. According to the Mishnah, the school of Shammai held that only sexual unfaithfulness justified divorce, while the school of Hillel allowed divorce for almost any cause, even a spoiled meal. The question whether a man may divorce his wife for any reason asks Jesus to take a side. The debate had political edges as well: Antipas's own divorce and remarriage had cost John the Baptist his life, and this conversation takes place in Antipas's territory.

In Jewish law a husband could divorce his wife, but a wife generally could not divorce her husband. The certificate of divorce protected the woman by declaring her free to remarry. Mark 10:1-31 and Luke 18:15-30 give parallels, and Mark 10:11-12 and Luke 16:18 record Jesus' teaching on divorce without the exception clause found in Matthew 5:32 and 19:9.
cultural:
In the ancient world marriage was arranged by families, and a divorced woman without a family to return to could face poverty, which gives weight to Jesus' refusal to treat divorce lightly. Eunuchs were men who had been castrated, often as servants in royal courts, and in Israel they were excluded from the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:1), though Isaiah 56:3-5 promised them a name better than sons and daughters. Jesus uses the word in three senses: those born unable to marry, those made so by others, and those who choose to forgo marriage for the kingdom.

Parents brought children to respected teachers for a blessing, and the disciples' rebuke reflects children's low status. Wealth was widely regarded as a sign of God's favor, which explains the disciples' astonishment in verse 25: if the rich cannot be saved, who can? The camel was the largest animal in Palestine and the eye of a needle the smallest opening, so the saying is deliberate hyperbole for the impossible. The popular idea that the needle's eye was a small gate in Jerusalem's wall has no ancient evidence behind it and misses the point that Jesus is describing something only God can do.
literary: The chapter has three units, each prompted by a question or approach: the Pharisees on divorce (verses 3 to 12), the children brought for blessing (verses 13 to 15), and the rich young man and the discussion that follows (verses 16 to 30). The divorce debate follows a common pattern of controversy: a testing question, an answer from Scripture (Genesis 1:27 and 2:24), a counter-question from Moses' law, a ruling, and a private explanation to disciples. The rich man's story turns on the word good and on the question of what is still lacking. The man asks about doing a good thing; Jesus points him to the One who is good. Jesus lists commandments from the second table of the law (duties to neighbor) and adds love for neighbor from Leviticus 19:18. The closing saying about first and last (verse 30) is repeated in reverse at 20:16, framing the parable of the vineyard workers.

outline.t: Jesus leaves Galilee for Judea beyond the Jordan
Marriage and those who forgo it for the kingdom
Riches and the kingdom: impossible with man
The reward of those who follow

doctrines.note: Jesus grounds marriage in creation: God made humanity male and female and joined husband and wife as one flesh. Marriage is God's work, not merely a human agreement, and Jesus treats its permanence as the norm. He also honors those who forgo marriage for the kingdom and welcomes children as models of the kingdom.
Jesus appeals behind Moses to the beginning, to God's design in Genesis 1 and 2. The law's concessions to hardness of heart do not define God's intent; the created order does.

The rich young man asks what good thing he must do to obtain eternal life. The disciples' question “Who then can be saved?” gets the answer that with man it is impossible but with God all things are possible. Entrance into the kingdom is God's gift, not a human achievement.
The kingdom reverses human rankings: children receive it, the rich struggle to enter, and the first will be last. Jesus promises a future renewal of all things in which his followers share his reign.

words.note: Porneia, sexual immorality, a broad term for sexual sin. Scholars debate whether in verse 9 it means adultery specifically, sexual sin more generally, or a marriage unlawful from the start (such as within forbidden degrees of kinship). The meaning of this one word shapes how traditions read the exception clause.

Sklerokardia, hardness of heart. Jesus says Moses permitted divorce because of it. The law regulated a broken reality rather than approving it. The word recalls the prophets' language for Israel's stubbornness and their hope that God would replace hearts of stone with hearts of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26).

Teleios, perfect, complete, mature. The same word appears in 5:48. In verse 21 it does not mean sinless but whole, undivided in devotion. What the young man lacks is not another rule kept but a heart free to follow Jesus.

Palingenesia, renewal or rebirth, literally becoming again. Here it means the renewal of all things at the end of the age, when the Son of Man sits on his glorious throne. It is used elsewhere in the New Testament only in Titus 3:5, of the washing of rebirth.

christ: Jesus speaks as one with authority over the law of Moses, interpreting it by God's purpose in creation. When the rich man calls a thing good, Jesus answers “There is only One who is good,” which in Matthew is not a denial of Jesus' goodness but a redirection to God, and then tells him to follow Jesus himself, placing loyalty to Jesus at the center of what God requires. His welcome of children reflects the character of the God who defends the weak. The promise that the Son of Man will sit on his glorious throne, with the twelve judging Israel's tribes, draws on Daniel 7, where one like a son of man receives dominion and the saints share the kingdom. The one who will sit on that throne is the one on his way to die, and the reversal of first and last is lived out first in him.

hard.q: Does Jesus allow divorce and remarriage, and if so, when?
hard.a: Christians who share a high view of marriage read verse 9 and its exception clause differently. Many Protestants have held that the exception permits divorce, and remarriage for the innocent party, when a spouse has committed adultery or serious sexual sin; many also add desertion, drawing on 1 Corinthians 7:15. The Catholic Church teaches that a valid, consummated sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved; it reads porneia as referring to unions that were unlawful from the start, and it permits separation in serious cases and declarations of nullity where a true marriage never existed, but not remarriage while a spouse lives. The Orthodox churches hold marriage to be permanent in principle but, as an act of pastoral mercy, permit divorce for serious causes including adultery, and allow a second or even third marriage with a service marked by repentance. Some scholars hold that Jesus, speaking to the Hillel-Shammai debate, forbade easy divorce without addressing every hard case, such as abuse or abandonment, which the church must weigh with care. All traditions agree that Jesus sets God's design above human convenience, and that the church must care for those whose marriages have broken, many of whom did not choose it. A spouse in danger of abuse is not required by this passage to remain in harm's way.

questions: Jesus appeals to the beginning to answer a question about his own day. How does God's original design shape how you think about marriage, singleness, or your own relationships?
The young man asked what he still lacked. If you asked Jesus that question, what do you think he might say?
The disciples were astonished that the rich might not be saved. In what ways does wealth, or the desire for it, compete with following Jesus in your life?
